The command line now honours the same environment variables the server has always honoured, so if you have one of them set and were relying on the old behaviour of using the home directory regardless, the database, the cluster and the configuration will be found in the place the variable names. This is the intended fix rather than a side effect, but it is a move.

## [15.4.0] - 2026-08-22

Closing the application no longer stops the database in the middle of what it was doing. On Windows the launcher ended the backend by ending its process tree, which is an unclean stop for PostgreSQL, and it did that on every ordinary close rather than only during an upgrade. The next start then had to replay the write-ahead log before it could do anything else, and for a large database that replay is long enough to look like an application that will not open. The launcher now asks the backend to stop over a loopback endpoint that only the launcher can reach, waits for it, and falls back to ending the process tree only when that fails. On a machine that has run an earlier version the clean stop needed one more thing before it could happen at all: the database library records every process that opens the cluster and stops the server on exit only when the list it reads back names the exiting process alone, it never removes a process that was killed rather than allowed to exit, and ending the process tree is exactly that kind of killing. So every existing install already carries a list naming processes that no longer exist, and the clean stop would have been skipped on precisely the machines it was written for, and skipped silently, because from outside a skipped stop and a completed one look the same. Those entries are now dropped on the way out, and only when the process named is demonstrably gone, since removing one that is alive would stop the database underneath something still using it. The endpoint refuses anything that is not a loopback request carrying the secret the launcher was started with, compared in constant time so the secret cannot be learned by timing, and it refuses every request outright unless this is a desktop install. Installing and uninstalling stopped being violent in the same way: the installer used to end every process on the machine that shared our executable name, which reached not only a second copy of the product that had nothing to do with the install being performed but every signed in user's session on that machine, and it now stops only processes running out of the directory being installed to, asking them to close before it insists.

Starting up no longer gives up on a database that is working. The launcher measured how long the backend had been starting and abandoned it at a fixed deadline, which is the wrong question to ask of a database replaying its log, because that work takes as long as it takes and says nothing while it does. It now measures silence instead, and recovery reports its progress every fifteen seconds with a countdown, so the launcher keeps waiting while the backend is still reporting progress and gives up only after four minutes of complete silence. The twenty minute ceiling is unchanged and still catches a backend that talks forever without ever becoming healthy, it simply stopped being the usual reason for giving up. When the launcher does give up it now says which step it was on, in words, rather than reporting that the backend did not start in time.

Modules can now be installed and removed from Settings, and chosen during onboarding. The capability existed and was reachable only by someone who knew the API. Settings gains a Modules tab that lists what is installed, groups it by category, shows what depends on what before a removal takes anything else with it, and says plainly when the current account may look but not change: the control is inert rather than present and then refused, and the endpoint refuses the same account independently, so the two agree. Switching a module off takes effect in the running process rather than at the next start, which is the difference between the feature working and looking like it works. Onboarding gains a picker, grouped by the work each module does, so a new instance starts with the modules that team actually uses instead of everything. The two are deliberately different things and the wording says so: onboarding chooses what appears in your own menu, Settings installs and removes for the whole instance, and conflating them is what previously made a module look switched off while it was still running.

A geographic information system can now read the project directly. The platform serves OGC API - Features over the data it already holds, so QGIS connects to it as a data source with no export step and no copy that can go stale: project anchors, map overlays exploded into their member features, and viewpoints, each filtered by what the account may see and each declaring whether it is project scoped rather than leaving a client to guess. The basemap tile endpoint is now part of the published interface instead of being hidden from the schema. Alongside it, a non-conformity can carry the coordinates it was raised at, and raising one puts a pin on the map, which is the loop a site inspector needs: stand at the defect, record it once, and have it appear both on the map and in the register.

Two authorisation defects are closed. Seven endpoints that write the exchange rates, work calendars and tax configurations required an account to be signed in and never checked what that account was allowed to do, and those rows are global to the installation rather than belonging to a tenant, so any account of any role could change the VAT rate and the currency conversion every estimate and invoice in the install computes from. In the same file the one action that could destroy nothing, fetching published rates from the central bank, was the one that was authorised. Separately, four endpoints answered anyone who asked. Two returned absolute server paths in their diagnostics, and they now require a permission and no longer name the path at all, because a caller entitled to the answer is still not entitled to the layout of our disk. One force-ran a converter binary for any stranger who sent the request, deliberately bypassing the cache that exists to stop exactly that, while every other route in the same file was already gated. The fourth polled a background job and was the only route in its file carrying no gate of any kind: an opaque task identifier is not a permission, it made the route a capability URL by accident, and it leaked whichever way that identifier travelled. It now asks for the same three things its two siblings had asked for all along. A neighbouring listing was looked at and deliberately left open, because it only reports whether files are present and gating it was never the fix.

An invoice in a currency written without decimals now adds up. Amounts were rounded on their way onto the page but added up before they were rounded, and rounding and addition do not commute once a line carries anything below the smallest unit the currency has. So three lines of a hundred were written as a hundred each and totalled as three hundred and one, and a receiver adding up the lines it was given got a different number from the total we sent. The European standard compares those figures exactly, with no tolerance, so the document was rejected on arrival. It was not only the line totals: the tax base and the amount due were wrong the same way and for the same reason, and across a sweep of three hundred and twelve documents two thirds of the failures were in those two rules rather than in the line sum. It affected every zero-decimal currency identically, which is what identifies it as a fault in how the document is written rather than a disagreement about any one currency, and the fix reads whatever minor-unit count the currency is configured with rather than hard-coding one. Our own validator could not see any of it, because it added the figures up itself and rounded once at the end, which is not what a receiver does: a receiver rounds nothing, it adds up the strings it was handed. Now that the amounts leave us already at the smallest unit, the two arithmetics agree.

Events that other parts of the system react to are now published after the work is saved rather than while it is still being saved. A subscriber opens its own database session, and a session cannot see rows another session has not committed, so a subscriber that wrote something pointing back at the new record failed on a constraint and the failure was logged at a level nobody reads. Seeded and imported data lost rows this way without anything appearing to go wrong. The publish now waits for the commit, and the events that carry a reference to their parent were moved over first.

The embedded database's recovery no longer trusts a guess. Before deciding whether a leftover process is the cluster it is looking for, it asks that process what it is holding. The previous check read the machine-wide table of network connections, which needs administrator rights on macOS and returns nothing useful for a cluster that listens on a Unix socket rather than a port, which is how the cluster runs on both macOS and Linux. On those platforms the check silently fell through to comparing process names, and the process it was asked about is not called postgres.

Elsewhere in this release: a coordination export can be limited to the topics that were selected, and a topic can be addressed by the identifier the format itself gives it rather than only by ours; the dashboard lists answer for the project in the address bar; a defects liability entry can record which statutory regime its limitation period comes from, so the date it produces can be justified rather than asserted; a tender award record is assembled from the procedure and says what is missing rather than quietly leaving it out; the change order trail names who submitted and who approved; feet and inches are read the way a drawing writes them; uploads written before upload roots were anchored on the data directory are still readable; and the marketing site now describes the programme and schedule work in the words planners use, in all thirty-seven languages, having previously said Gantt once and nothing else.

One note for installations upgraded with pip. This is the first release whose published package carries the migration tree, so `alembic upgrade head` becomes possible on a pip installation for the first time. Start the application once before running it. Earlier packages could not record which migrations a database had already received, so a database created by one of them looks, to the migration tool, like a database that has had none of them, and running the tool first walks the whole history against tables that already exist and stops with an error. Starting the application first brings the schema up to date and records that, so the command becomes a correct no operation instead of a failure. Nothing is lost either way, because the attempt runs in a single transaction and rolls itself back, but the order saves you the failure. Installations that run from source or from the container image are already recorded and are not affected.

## [15.3.1] - 2026-08-21

The screen that appears while the application is starting now names the version it is running. Someone whose application will not open has no other way to find that out, because the About screen lives inside the application they cannot reach, and by then the installer is usually long gone from their downloads. This matters because the message shown when starting fails is deliberately general: the same sentence about the backend not starting in time is produced by a fault that was corrected several releases ago and by one that is still open, and nothing in the report told the two apart. A report could arrive complete and carefully written and still not be answerable. The version now appears on the screen itself and as the second line of the details the copy button produces, directly under the heading and above the path to the log file, and it is written from the moment the screen first appears rather than only after something has gone wrong.

An application that was starting normally is no longer given up on while it is still working. The window the launcher allowed for the whole of startup was the same length as the budget the backend allows for bringing the local database up on its own, so a database that spent that budget recovering left nothing at all for everything that follows it: migrations, loading the modules, creating the tables and preparing first-run data. That ordering was not a remote possibility. The installer stops a running copy by ending its process tree, which stops the local database without letting it close cleanly, so the first start after an upgrade is exactly the log replay the budget exists for. The application was healthy and still working, and it was reported as one that had not started, and starting it again produced the same thing because nothing had actually gone wrong to clear. The window is now twice the budget it waits on, which leaves a comfortable margin and costs nothing when a start has genuinely failed, since that is reported the moment it happens rather than when the window closes.

## [15.3.0] - 2026-08-21

A desktop application that had stopped starting, on a machine where nothing was wrong with the installation, starts again. A run that fails after bringing the local database up leaves that database running behind it. The next start found it and asked whether it was there by opening a connection, and opening a connection proves that something is holding the address rather than that a database is behind it. Those two come apart in exactly this case: the process was still there and could no longer answer. So the application announced the local database as ready and then failed every request it made to it in the same breath, and it did so on every start after that, because nothing it could do would clear what was in the way. Reinstalling did not help, since nothing about the installation was wrong. The database is now asked a question it has to answer rather than one it only has to accept, and every answer counts, including a refusal to serve, because a refusal is still proof that something is there to refuse. One that has stopped answering is cleared away so a working one can take its place. A database still replaying its log after an unclean shutdown is not touched by any of this and is waited for exactly as before. Anyone whose application stopped starting after the upgrade to 15.0.0 gets it back without having to do anything.

Starting the local database on Windows no longer fails on a directory the application had just made for it. The database's own setup program takes a different path when the directory it is pointed at is already there, beginning by correcting the permissions on it, and that correction is the one thing it cannot do: it re-runs itself under a restricted account so that a database is never owned by an administrator, and the account it becomes is not always allowed to change a directory an administrator created. It is now handed a path that does not exist yet, so it makes the directory, owns what it made, and touches nothing of ours. An installation that already has a database is unaffected, since that directory is there either way.

An entry that cannot be written to the activity record stops taking the work it was describing with it. A record of what happened is written in the same breath as the thing that happened, which is what makes it trustworthy, but one bad entry was ending the whole transaction rather than only itself, so a single unwritable line about a change could discard the change. The record keeps that property and no longer holds the work hostage to it.

An installation told not to fetch the search model no longer fetches it. The switch that says so was read by the part that installs the model and not by the part that loads it, so a machine on a closed network still went looking, and what the operator got was a long wait ending in a network error rather than the immediate and honest answer that this installation does not do semantic search. A model already present is still used.

An installation can be asked what state the semantic search encoder is in, and told to fetch it. The weights are a large download, so an installation may already hold them, may be fetching them now, may have tried and failed, or may have been told not to want them at all, and until now the only way to tell those four apart was to run a search and read what came back. Both answers are available directly. Asking costs nothing, because the question is answered without loading the model, which makes it safe to ask on a timer while a download runs. Starting the fetch returns straight away rather than holding the request open for the length of the transfer, and an installation that cannot download says so in the state it returns instead of through a failure.

A database carried across an upgrade keeps the moments it already recorded. The column holding when a project route was classified was created before the application declared that it stores a point in time rather than a wall clock reading, and a fresh installation has had the right kind of column for a while, so the difference could only show on a machine that had been running for longer. On those, the stored value was read back in whatever time zone the database session happened to be in, which moves a recorded moment by the offset of the server instead of leaving it where it was put. The column is now widened on start, reading what is already in it as UTC, so the times survive the change rather than drift by it. An installation that already has the right column is left alone.

Four boxes in the electronic invoice clearance panel get their background back. They named colours the palette does not define, so a warning, a success and a rejection each drew as bare text inside a border instead of the tinted block the rest of the application uses for those same three meanings.

## [15.2.0] - 2026-08-20

Installing the desktop application no longer depends on the machine reaching Microsoft. The installer carried a small downloader for the web view runtime and fetched it during setup, so a site office behind a closed network met a failure about a component rather than about the network it was actually short of. It now carries the runtime itself. Windows also stops offering two installers for one application. The .msi and the .exe put the same product in the same directory while each kept its own record of having done so, which made taking one and later the other a way to have the application listed twice, and the gates that demanded both went in the same change as the format they demanded. If the copy you have came from the .msi, remove that entry before running the .exe; your data lives outside the installed folder and an uninstall does not touch it.

A desktop application that cannot serve now says so rather than sitting there. The startup check answered two ways, ready or not yet, so a server that had started and was reporting that it could not do its job was indistinguishable from one still coming up, and the window opened on top of it. What the person got was a shell whose every action failed, which is how a problem with an installation came to look like a broken product. A backend that answers and declares itself unfit is now a third answer, and it is shown with the reason the backend gave instead of arriving much later as a timeout that explains nothing. One that has gone quiet is still read as starting or dying rather than as degraded, so a single bad reading is not held against the next one, and a probe that is accepted and then never answered no longer holds the wait open for as long as it likes.

The update notice stops sending people to a page to hunt through. It names the installer that fits the machine it is running on, because the release lists what it carries and the browser knows which computer it is. A phone is offered nothing rather than a package for a desktop it is not. Where the release has no file for that platform, and the Fedora package is allowed to be absent by design, the release page remains as the answer rather than a broken link. The check itself now goes to this installation's own server instead of to GitHub from every browser tab, so an office behind one address stops exhausting an hourly limit meant for one visitor and reading, correctly and uselessly, that there is no update.

An order raised against a bill position now commits against the money the estimate priced. The reading side of that had been complete for a long time and nothing ever wrote the link, so committed against remaining was zero on every project: four hundred cubic metres of concrete could be on order and the line for it still read as entirely uncommitted. The buyer is not asked what a cost line is, the position resolves to one. Correcting a quantity keeps the link, which is worth saying separately because an order is rebuilt from its lines when it is edited, and a version of this that only handled the first draft would have looked right and quietly emptied the report on the first correction.

Beside it, a bill position can be asked what actually happened to it, in one row: what the estimate said, what the budget planned, what is committed and contracted, what has been installed and what has been consumed from the store. A position nobody has reported on says so rather than drawing zero progress, because never reported and reported as none are different facts, and an order beyond its estimate reads as negative rather than as merely complete.

Post-calculation reads the finished job back against what it was priced at, and it now covers material as well as labour. An earned total may only be set against an actual that covers the same lines: comparing a full estimate with a partial record of what was spent produces a margin that looks like a result and is an artefact of the gap, so where the two do not cover the same ground the page says which lines are missing rather than dividing anyway. The screen also states its own name in the top bar in every language now, which it did not before, because the heading a screen reader was given had been translated while the name a sighted reader saw was the English literal.

Six modules gained the data they were always drawn against, and this is the part to read carefully, because what landed is the substance and not yet the screen. A basis of estimate can now carry the number, where it came from and how accurate it claims to be. A project roster can say who is on the job and in what capacity. A design option can be compared on time and carbon rather than on cost alone. Formwork can be recorded as a system chosen rather than only as a price. A delivery can be booked against the bill positions it carries, and a stock movement can be tied to the position that priced the material, so what left the store can be set against what was measured. All of that is reachable through the API in this version. The screens for it follow in the next one, because putting them in front of people before every language has the words for them would mean showing most of the world a list of key names instead of a form.

## [15.1.0] - 2026-08-20

The Windows desktop application of 15.0.0 did not start. It stopped with a missing locales directory before it ever drew a window, on every machine, and reinstalling could not help because the directory was absent from the build itself. The catalogue the server reads while starting sits beside the application package rather than inside it, so packaging the package left it behind. The wheel force-included it and the frozen bundle did not, which is why the same version installed from PyPI worked and the desktop build did not. The bundle carries it now, and a test refuses any release whose frozen build ships less than the wheel declares.

Everything else that could stop a first start went with it. The server starts somewhere it is allowed to write instead of beside its own executable, which is read only under Program Files. It no longer believes a pidfile whose number has since been handed to something else, so a machine that was shut down mid-run starts cleanly rather than waiting on a process that is not ours. It announces the local database only once something answers on it, and it asks the cluster on the address family the cluster is actually listening on, so a first run on a host with no IPv6 loopback no longer times out against a database that was up the whole time. The command line asks about the database the product really uses rather than the one it used to.

A data directory the bundled PostgreSQL cannot open is now refused before anything touches it, and the refusal says which major was found, which was expected and where it lives. It offers the routes that keep the data first and names the destructive one last, carrying its own warning, because a major version move used to arrive three retries deep as a connection error with nothing in it about versions, and reinstalling made it no better.

Release 15.0.0 shipped without its signature, checksums, software bill of materials and rpm, because the signing job asked the desktop build for a verdict and that run ended cancelled. The artefacts existed; the sentence about them did not. Signing now reads the assets a run produced, an inventory step refuses a release with a platform missing, and a failed read of the asset list is reported as not measured rather than as a judgement.

Away from the desktop, the activity trail keeps the deletions it was silently dropping, because a bill's audit entry named the bill by a column carrying a foreign key and the row was already gone by the time the entry was written. A budget is judged by what the job will finish at rather than by what has been invoiced so far. Brazilian demo bills are written with the letters they are written with, American English answers the British spellings an American reader trips on, and the demo correspondence register belongs to the project it sits in rather than repeating one fixed list of letters in every project on the platform. The BCF issue register stopped drawing three different nothings as one broken picture: a snapshot that will not load keeps the crossed-out glyph, a viewpoint carrying no image gets a crosshair because the schema makes the image optional, and an issue raised outside a viewer gets neither.

## [15.0.0] - 2026-08-19

The product crosses into two markets it could previously only describe. Nine playbooks written for the American market ship beside twelve written for the German one, and behind them sit the things those markets actually turn on: Texas and California packs carrying their own state rules, a weekly certified payroll for public works, the statutory payment clocks of VOB/B and BGB, and the working time record MiLoG section 17 requires, shown on the timesheet where the hours are entered rather than in a report nobody opens. American English is a locale of its own now rather than a spelling variant, and a bill of quantities is a Bid Schedule to the reader who calls it that.

GAEB is no longer an import format with an export bolted to it. A plain X84 export is a Hauptangebot, alternate bids opt in rather than being guessed at, the Pruefdatei survives a round trip, imported sections keep their hierarchy on every screen that shows them, and umlauts survive the filename. A bill states only what it can state: the export summary stopped claiming prices for a bill that carries none, an unpriced Zuschlagsposition is a position and not an import error, and a long text with a graphic embedded in it is capped rather than allowed to bounce the position it belongs to. Typed units resolve the way the person typing them means them: a ton entered in an American bill is the short ton, and cf reaches cubic feet the way sf already reached square feet.

Markups became something an estimator can reason about. A section carries its own rate, an exception is drawn as an exception instead of being folded into the stack that contradicts it, a bond is priced off its rate card and an escalation off an index, and the contingency stays out of a base that already carries profit. Where the stack does not add up the product says so and lets the estimator proceed, because a markup engine that refuses is a markup engine people work around. One country now yields one markup stack whichever engine is asked.

A register that cannot fit on one screen now says so, and the programme to make that true everywhere has a ratchet behind it. A list that would not fit used to look complete, and the answer is not a message on one screen but a rule across the product: the count comes from the register rather than from the page, a filter cannot deny what the register holds, an empty screen is no longer reported as an empty register, and a guard runs at commit time so a new list cannot ship silently truncated. Around thirty registers gained the notice this release, among them the quality registers, correspondence, inspections, the resource roster, the diary, contracts, the snag list and the risk section. The honest figure for the rest is 484: that is how many list endpoints the guard still counts as waiting, and it is printed by the guard rather than estimated here. What is finished is the rule and the ratchet, not the sweep.

Measurement from drawings is real work now rather than a demonstration. The seeded German floor plans carry verifiable quantities and a second issue so revisions can be compared, calibration is stated in the reader's units and digits, every quantity readout goes through one locale aware formatter, and a takeoff position links to a priced line only where the unit can actually be reached. The viewer follows the document's own project instead of whichever project the switcher last remembered.

Language reaches further in and stops leaking. Forty one locales carry the product, module manifests introduce themselves in the reader's language rather than in English, page headings and the browser tab follow the language the rest of the screen speaks, and the first paint waits for the active bundle instead of showing English for a moment. Numbers stop asking the browser which language they are in. A figure written with no locale takes the operating system's language rather than the one the reader chose, so a German running an English Windows read a German page with American separators and nothing about that was visible to whoever wrote the line. The shared formatter and 218 screens behind it now name the app locale, percentages, compact money and measurements included, and a test names every call site that still asks the browser. Ukrainian and American English joined the repository. Uzbek is in the tree and deliberately not in the picker, because roughly a fifth of it still reads as English, and a language offered half translated is worse than a language not yet offered.

A first visit is 14.9 MB lighter. The service worker keeps locale catalogues out of what it downloads up front, and six of them were slipping through on a naming rule that assumed a language code is two letters. American English and the Spanish, Portuguese and Filipino variants are not, so five full catalogues and an overlay were being handed to every visitor by the very lane written to prevent exactly that.

Semantic search stops being an install time decision. The encoder downloads in the background and reports which of five states it is in, the setup wizard shows the download rather than performing it silently, and the desktop build ships the encoder it was already fetching, on the CPU build of torch rather than the CUDA one. A reindex that wrote nothing is reported as having written nothing.

An API key is honoured at the permissions it declares, a self hosted AI endpoint belongs to the user who saved it, and three company registers stopped presenting themselves as project scoped while a register scoped to a project is now read from the project the route names. Four security advisories reported against earlier versions are fixed in this tree, and the most recent of them, an AI endpoint hijacking issue reported on 2026-08-10, reaches a tagged release for the first time here.

Reliability work that has no screen of its own. Three Alembic revisions the chain pointed at and did not have were restored, a healed sequence column is numbered the way the migration numbers it, starting the app twice no longer binds every handler twice, exports carry real filenames through every download header, and the environment doctor now proves a native extra by importing it instead of locating a directory, gives the desktop build advice it can act on, and spends one line rather than a whole report on a check that could not run.

## [14.8.1] - 2026-08-12

The file module is called Documents everywhere the product names it. It had drifted into three names across the sidebar, the case chips and the module catalog, and the catalog key had gone out translated into none of the forty languages. The rename is now finished in every locale, and a module can say its own name in the reader's language, so an installed register introduces itself the way the rest of the product speaks.

An electronic invoice reads the buyer's address from the contact the invoice already names instead of asking for it a second time, and findings about that buyer are raised on the screen that now holds the buyer rather than the one that used to. The German profile checks follow the published rules to the letter, an address that is only a country is refused rather than exported, and clearance clears the invoice the customer was billed, not a flattened copy of it.

Every desktop release answers for its own signature. A backfill can sign bytes that already shipped without minting a new component list, the workflow reads the signature back off the release rather than inferring it from its own configuration, an unsigned Windows build says so, and a failed build leg can no longer silence the signing job behind it.

A list that could not fit on one screen used to look complete. The schedule reports how many rows exist rather than how many fit, list totals stop being dropped behind the page envelope in the modules that carry one, the truncation notice speaks the showing count line every locale already has, and a guard runs at commit time and in the hygiene lane so a new list cannot ship silently truncated again.

The product serves its own typefaces and no longer claims a script the bundled fonts cannot draw. Mongolian is withdrawn from the language picker until it gets a native pass: the file stays, the offer goes. The four Spanish locales got back the diacritics they had been carrying as bare letters, Portuguese and Brazilian Portuguese got theirs, es-CO and es-CL ran the substitutions their own headers had documented but never executed, and the ten newest case playbooks got their English copy written.

Deferred background work no longer borrows the app's database connections into a rival event loop, an interrupted currency backfill keeps what it already filled, and the migration lane refuses a data rewrite that carries no acknowledgement of the table it grows.

## [14.8.0] - 2026-08-11

A foreman in a basement or a lift shaft has no signal, and the hours still have to reach the office. The device keeps the day in a local queue and replays it when there is one. Replay is at least once by construction, because a reconnect can fire twice and a request whose response was lost is indistinguishable from one that never arrived, so every logical day carries a key minted on the device and a redelivery returns the timesheet the first delivery produced instead of writing a second one. An operation carries the entry's whole state rather than a difference against what the server holds, which is what makes a replayed correction safe without a revision counter to compare it against.

The compliance panel had been reporting fatal EN 16931 violations for seller identity, for the tax registration behind it and for the bank account, and none of the three had anywhere to be entered. Naming a problem the product offers no way to solve moves the dead end further along instead of removing it. These are properties of the company running the instance and identical on every invoice it issues, so they are held once and merged beneath whatever an individual invoice says for itself. Both places that render an EN 16931 document resolve the same configuration, so one invoice row cannot produce two different documents. The bank account is checked against its own ISO 7064 check digits on the way in, because that is the last point where a mistyped account can be caught at all: the receiver's validator checks that the document is well formed, not that the account exists, so a wrong digit yields a perfectly valid invoice that simply never gets paid. An account from a country outside the length table is accepted on its check digits alone, since a table that has fallen behind the registry must not be able to tell a firm its own bank account does not exist.

An e-invoice named Germany for a company that never chose a country. The party record defaulted to DE, the mapper substituted DE for a seller or a buyer that named none, and both writers substituted it once more on the way into the XML. A firm that never opened the e-invoice settings therefore issued documents declaring it established in Germany, and the rule written to catch exactly that could never fire, because BR-9 and BR-11 test for an empty country and nothing was empty by the time they ran. Seller country is BT-40 and buyer country is BT-55, both mandatory under EN 16931, and a document that names the wrong one is a false statement about where a legal person is established. The country now stays empty from the stored settings through to the model, so the rules fire and the message names the screen to open. A strict render refuses through the gate that was already there; a best effort render omits the element rather than filling it, and drops the wrapper around it too, because an empty wrapper reads as a malformed address rather than as an address with no country. The same defaulting sat one line away on the currency, where an unset currency was rendered as EUR and would have put figures on the document in a currency nobody chose, and that is gone as well.

This changes what an export does, so it is worth knowing before upgrading. The standing settings carry seller fields only, so an invoice that never named a buyer country used to export and is now refused under BR-11 until the country is filled in. That refusal is the point of the rule. The finding it raises was also sending people to the wrong place: BR-9 and BR-11 shared one sentence naming the e-invoice settings, which is right for the seller, whose country is configured there once, and wrong for the buyer, whose country belongs on the invoice. The buyer message now says so, in the same words the export route already uses when it refuses.

Overdue deadline notifications reached nobody, on any project. The sweep chose who to notify with a format check, so a well formed identifier that no user is behind was taken as the owner and the managers fallback never ran. The write then broke the notification foreign key, and because a failed flush leaves the session unusable, every later item in the same pass failed too. One unresolvable row therefore silenced the whole sweep, on every tick. Being a real user now means being present in the users table, and each item runs in its own savepoint so a row that cannot be written rolls back alone and the pass carries on.

The e-invoice settings screen could not be opened on the rows it exists to repair. The read schema inherited the write schema, so every rule that governs typing a value also ran when handing one back, and a row holding something the form would refuse answered with a validation error instead of the stored value. Rows like that arrive from an import, a restore or a hand run update, so the form is not the only way in. Reading no longer normalises either: a country code stored in lower case comes back in lower case rather than being shown corrected while the row still holds the old value.

The compliance panel claimed a verdict it could not reach. It said an invoice satisfies every rule of the selected profile and is ready to send. This build implements roughly forty EN 16931 and XRechnung rules by hand, the profiles carry many times that, and the authority on whether a document is accepted is the receiver's own validator, which we do not run and deliberately do not vendor.

Portuguese now reads as Portuguese. pt and pt-BR agreed byte for byte on 670 values carrying an unambiguously Brazilian form, so a reader in Portugal was shown Brazilian wording throughout the product. Seven word families, among them the words for record, planning, portfolio, user, team and container, are in their European forms across every inflection and capitalisation. 671 values changed and not one key: the key set, the key order and the count are exactly what they were, which is what makes this a change of wording rather than of structure.

Sixty-five shared keys said different things in different languages. Where one English string is rendered across twenty-one locales, translations had settled into two or three competing renderings of the same term, so a control was named one way on one screen and another way on the next. Each of the sixty-five was decided rather than mechanically unified, because one English term can carry two settled renderings inside a single language and the right one sometimes depends on where the string appears. What was decided, and why, is written down beside the result.

## [14.7.0] - 2026-08-11

A register can be described inside the product and exist a moment later. The builder collects what the record has to hold over four steps, shows every file it would write before a single one is written, and installs on a press, into a module directory belonging to the instance rather than into the platform source tree, so an upgrade cannot carry a user module away with it and a packaged build finally has somewhere to put one. The module loads straight after, so there is no restart to plan and no second switch to find: the review step is the confirmation, and this is the one place in the product where a confirmed result takes effect immediately. What the assistant drafts is the description and never the Python, so the worst a bad draft can do is describe something the specification layer refuses. A module installed at runtime cannot ship a compiled screen, so each one serves its own specification and a single screen renders the list, the detail and the form out of it. That screen pages and keeps the total on screen at all times rather than once the list overflows, because nothing distinguishes these are all of them from these are the ones that fit, and that is the one failure a register must not have. Search pulls the remaining pages in before it answers, since a search over a partly loaded register reports nothing found about rows it never read, which is a wrong answer rather than an incomplete one. A generated module creates its own table from the same model the code reads, has its identifiers checked against the shape of an identifier and against the names the generated row already uses, and is refused if the linter the platform already installs would refuse it. The wizard draws the table being described while it is being described, in bars rather than in sample values, because an invented row reads as a real one on the very screen where somebody decides whether the module is right.

Disabling a module takes its routes down again. Removal worked by filtering the application's route table on the path of each entry, which was true while including a router copied its routes into that table. It no longer copies, so the filter matched nothing, removed nothing, logged that it had removed them, and every endpoint of the disabled module kept answering until the process restarted, taking the builder's own uninstall with it. Routers are found by identity now, the published schema is regenerated so it stops describing a module that is gone, and the two other readers of that table are corrected the same way, one of which had been answering no about a mounted module and mounting it a second time on every enable.

Every mounted module has a way in from the product. The previous release said the three statutory modules answered over the API with no screens and that their screens were the next wave, and they have them. The payment clock leads with the answer the module exists to give, which is the sum payable and the reason for it: where a valid payment notice was served that is the notified sum, and where the payer let the window close it is the sum applied for with no defence surviving. Reading a clock is what refreshes the breach register on the server, because a deadline passes whether or not anybody is looking, and a register that looks quiet on a project nobody opens is reporting the reading rather than the payments, which the screen says rather than implying all is well. Withholding tax leads with what a payment actually pays out and names the band it landed on rather than printing a bare figure, because a party whose verification has lapsed drops to the scheme default, which is the highest rate, and expiry is computed on every read so a standing that lapsed overnight is late on the screen the moment it is late in fact. Clearance records what a tax authority answered in the authority's own words, takes its regimes, statuses and installed adapters from the server rather than from lists written into the screen, and prints a rejection code verbatim because that code is what anybody investigating the invoice will ask for. A census of the 184 mounted routers against the whole frontend tree is what found them, and it found the rest as well. Cost matching, currencies and earned value had 47 endpoints between them and no route, no menu entry and no page, and each has one now: matching is queue led and two pass, so a run proposes and a person confirms, with the tier and the decision deliberately kept apart because a confident match is still a proposal. The inbound email reader was the last module no file under the frontend mentioned in any spelling. It shows each delay signal with the phrases that produced it, because a confidence with no evidence under it asks to be trusted rather than checked, and it says plainly that nothing is stored, since a reader who assumes the import was filed will go looking for it later.

An electronic invoice is now checked against the rules a receiver will actually cite, and it can be issued from a screen. The EN 16931 exporter could already produce XRechnung, Peppol and the hybrid PDF and nothing in the application reached it, so in practice this build could not issue an electronic invoice at all. An invoice row opens a panel that asks the server to check the document before anything is downloaded and renders the answer the way a receiver reads it. A fatal rule closes the download, because the file would be refused on arrival. An advisory rule leaves the download open and says what would make the invoice easier to process and pay. Both print the rule identifier beside the sentence, because BR-DE-15 is the string a tax portal quotes back at the sender and the prose is not, and showing the two in one undifferentiated list teaches people to ignore the list. Running a full rules engine would mean a runtime that does not fit the platform's memory budget, and the rules are small predicates over the semantic model, so they are expressed directly. Writing them down surfaced three live defects in shipped code: the payment means defaulted to credit transfer while neither builder ever wrote a payment account, so every document the module produced failed BR-61 on the default path; a VAT accounting currency was written without the VAT total in that currency, which BR-53 requires, leaving an amount in one currency to be read against another; and document amounts were quantized to two decimals whatever the currency, which printed cents on a yen invoice.

An invoice can carry a different VAT rate on every line, which a construction invoice routinely needs, because standard rated own works sit beside a subcontract under reverse charge or beside a reduced rate supply. One header rate applied to every line means a breakdown that misstates what was taxed at what rate, and a receiver either refuses it or books the wrong tax. The breakdown is one group per distinct rate and category pair now, each group's basis being exactly the lines that belong to it. Nothing is backfilled and the new columns are nullable, so a line written before this falls back to the invoice level rate and every invoice already issued renders the figures it rendered before, because inventing a rate for those rows would assert a tax treatment nobody entered.

The hybrid PDF relates its embedded invoice as an alternative rather than as data, which is what Factur-X 1.0 and ZUGFeRD 2.1 require, since the XML is the same invoice in another form and not a supplement to the page. A receiver that picks its attachment by relationship, which is what the specification tells it to do, would have found no invoice in a file that otherwise looks perfect: the document opens, the attachment is there, it carries the right name and the XML is valid. The test that existed read the attachment back by name and compared the bytes against the function that built them, so it was comparing a function with itself and could not see this. The export panel also stops offering the hybrid PDF on a profile that has no hybrid form, because that carrier is defined for one syntax only, and a button that can only fail reads as a supported export.

Two of the statutory modules were corrected while their screens were being built. A clearance document already sitting in submitted could be put through the whole of the send path, the duplicate lookup, the blocking rules, the full evaluation and the adapter registry, before the state machine refused it at the very end with a message describing the machinery rather than the mistake. Nothing ever reached a tax authority twice, but the refusal arrives up front now. And a withholding exemption limit is applied only where it and the payment are in one currency: the threshold was compared without either side's currency ever being asked for, so a payment of 4000 in one currency came back flagged as possibly exempt against a limit of 5000 in another. The flag changes no rate, which is why no arithmetic test could see it, and it is the sentence a payer reads before deciding whether to deduct at all.

A requirement can say why it exists, who asked for it, when it applies, how it would be proven and which work it governs. Stored as an entity, an attribute and a constraint, it states what is required and nothing about its life, and it could name exactly one priced position. Rationale, originator and originator role, phase and verification method are columns now, each held as a neutral key rather than a display word, so one row reads as the German fee stage in Germany and as the British work stage in Britain instead of being readable in one country and untranslatable everywhere else. The phase spine maps onto the German fee stages, the British work stages and the ISO 19650 delivery and operational phases, and a system is allowed to have no name for a phase rather than being forced into an equivalence the standards do not make. Which work a requirement governs moved to a table of its own, because one column could only ever hold the most recent position while a rule such as every exterior wall being fire rated governs every wall in the bill, and the reverse direction exists now too: open a bill item and see what it has to satisfy, which used to mean scanning every requirement in the project. Adding that table made the older single position route wrong without touching its own code, since linking one position and then another left the requirement naming the second with nothing remembering the first, and three separate counters measured coverage from the old column alone, so the coverage figure on the dashboard would have fallen as people moved to the attachment that holds more. A requirement set also carries the wording its project reads in, ISO 19650 or neutral, which renames concepts and never changes which ones exist, so it is safe to switch at any time.

A worker day is costed once, from whichever source recorded it. Three field surfaces record labour against a project, the diary, the daily report and the timesheet, and only the report reached the cost model, so a site that captured attendance on a phone and hours on a sheet showed a labour budget quietly short by whatever the other two carried. Approving a diary entry or a timesheet publishes the same labour event the report publishes, and because the same day can legitimately arrive from more than one of them, a worker day is claimed as it is costed and a second source naming the same person on the same date is named in the response rather than silently dropped, with the claim kept as a row so the reason a figure was left out survives the request that decided it. The undo path had to move with it. A reversal credits the figure that was actually posted rather than recomputing today's rate, which is what a rate edited between approval and reversal would otherwise leave behind, and it releases only its own claims, so a corrected sheet can cost the day the mistaken one had taken while a day another source is correctly costing stays taken. Approval itself is never blocked by any of this, because the manager in front of the sheet did not cause the overlap and cannot fix it from that screen. The crew screen also stopped refetching in a loop over the one connection it exists to work without, which came from a session reader building a fresh object on every call.

A tender in Chile, Colombia and Brazil is priced the way each country reads it. All three had a template and all three reached a total the same way everything else does, overhead then profit then tax on the lot, and that road gets the wrong number in each of them for a different reason. Chile has its own unit price analysis now, the form a public tender is submitted and compared in, with the direct cost split into labour, materials and plant, carrying contingency, overhead and profit in turn and leaving the tax outside the unit price where a tender expects it. Contingency ships at zero, because one invented at some plausible rate has to be noticed and removed by every project that does not carry one. Colombia quotes its markup as three shares of the direct cost, none of them compounding, and the tax on a construction contract for immovable property falls on the profit alone rather than on the contract value, which on a million pesos of direct cost is a difference of more than a fifth of the job. Brazil's tax term divides rather than adds, because those taxes are levied on the invoiced amount, the amount that already contains them, and a percentage of the subtotal under-recovers every time. Rather than bake a pre-grossed-up constant into a template, where it becomes a defect the moment a contractor types the nominal rate, the cascade engine learned a gross-up step of its own and refuses a rate of a hundred or more, since at that point there is no price left for the tax to be a share of. The flat templates all stay, because an internal budget priced flat is not wrong, and the catalogue now allows a country to appear under two methods and checks that when it does the two really compute differently. Chile and Colombia were also the two sizeable clearance regimes missing from the e-invoicing catalogue, and both are registered.

A currency with no minor unit is printed without one. A unit price analysis in Chilean pesos read 82000.00, and those two digits are not a rounding choice, they are a quantity the currency cannot express, on the one figure that goes into a public tender. Both currency tables already recorded it and neither was being asked: four server side renderers, the JSON view, the sheet view, the written analysis and the exported spreadsheet, each carried a hardcoded two decimals, as did the assembly screens. Fixing one of them would have left the file a contractor actually submits still printing cents, which is harder to notice than fixing none, so all of them take the precision from the currency now. Percentages keep two decimals whatever the currency, because a markup of 12.5 per cent is 12.5 per cent everywhere and rounding it to whole units would restate the contractor's own markup, and quantities keep four. The bill of quantities editor carried a worse version of the same fault: saving a resource into the user's own catalogue rebuilt the currency code from the display symbol, recognised three symbols and answered euro for everything else, so a project in several currencies wrote its catalogue rows in euros, and for the Chilean peso it was confidently wrong rather than merely wrong, because that symbol is a dollar sign. The project's own code was already to hand and simply was not used.

Repricing a region reaches the assemblies built on it. Three code paths write a cost item rate and two of them publish the event the assemblies side listens for. The third is the one that rewrites a whole region from the resource price sheet, and it published nothing, so a user moved the prices for a region, the cost items changed, and every assembly quoting them kept its own snapshot. A budget built from assemblies never saw the reprice, reported from an install where unit price analysis is the whole method and the stale copy is the number that goes into a tender. The event is published once for the region and after the commit, because a single run is capped at 250000 items and a fan out per item would be its own outage, and a subscriber opening its own session before the write lands reads the old rate and writes it straight back. A rate that cannot be read as a number leaves its row alone and is counted, since the obvious way to write that loop answers zero for anything it cannot parse, and one unreadable price would zero every component built on it and collapse the parent to nothing. The cost base picker also says how deep each catalogue goes, on a band of one to five with the work item count and the position in the family behind it, instead of offering nine national bases and nothing to choose between them but the country name.

A DXF opens without the converter binary it never needed. An upload was resolved through a format alias to the converter, which is published for one processor architecture only, so a self-hosted install on another could not open a DXF at all, even though the platform already reads DXF in pure Python for the takeoff module. The drawing data never needed that binary, only the DWG container does. The native reader writes the same element table a converter would have written, one row per entity, so the parser, the grouping, the column picker and the summary all work unchanged, and the three preflights that gate an upload on converter availability exempt a natively readable format rather than rejecting the file one call before the code that reads it. A drawing is also measured once rather than once per sheet it appears on. Entities came straight from the viewer parser, which returns every layout plus the contents of every block definition an insert references, so a plan that also sits inside a title block sheet was measured twice and a 50 square metre slab arrived in the bill as 100, with nothing in the table or the log to say why, while a door block was measured once as geometry on top of the inserts that place it and added an element nobody builds. The parse log now carries how many entities were measured out of how many were read and how many were unreadable, so a table built from a third of a drawing is visible rather than merely confident.

Three findings from an external tester's report on the drawing viewer are addressed. The hatch spacing was a literal that the pattern cache keyed on, so the pattern never answered the zoom at all: a hatched region drawn small received the same grid as one drawn large and filled in solid over the geometry underneath, which is why the overlaps went away when you zoomed in. The floating viewer controls were each anchored to the same corner region independently, so whichever one grew last covered its neighbour and a longer translation moved the collision to a different pair; they share one row across the top of the canvas now. And the viewer strokes a run of same-styled entities in a single path rather than opening and stroking one per entity, where before it set five or six context properties ahead of each of thousands of short segments that mostly agree about their colour. That is what drawing costs, and it is a separate thing from the frozen readouts that made the viewer look unresponsive, which are also fixed.

The demo estate stops opening on empty registers. Sixteen installed, routed and permissioned modules met every project with the same nothing here yet card, and each has a seeder now, derived from what the project already carries rather than authored, so the screens open on a register somebody could have kept. A seventeenth had been written complete and then never referenced by anything, so that module shipped empty while the code that would have filled it sat in the tree looking finished. Three seeders that had shipped for months covered the first three projects and read their marker off the first one, so seven of the ten demo projects were permanently without a federated model or a clash run, and because that marker made every later boot a no-op, no upgrade would ever have filled them. Safety gets a register of its own per project rather than seven registers shared across thirty four. Site preparation gets the mobilisation plan that the readiness rollup, the category breakdown and the commencement gate all count down to. The five hand-written projects that name a client, their subcontractors and their consultants but no main contractor now name one, because the registers seeded after them point at that role by default, so every punch item read as unassigned and both contract signature blocks named a company with no contact behind it. The German, Portuguese, Spanish and French seed text has its accents back, all 1385 spellings of them, because an estimator reads an ASCII transliteration as a typo and it is the first thing a visitor from that country sees.

Four modules have now been caught seeding values their own schema refuses, so that check is no longer written per module. It reads the vocabulary out of every module's schemas and attributes each seeded record to the module that owns it by key coverage, because a field name does not identify a vocabulary and priority means one scale on a task and another on a punch item. It runs in the lane that blocks a merge. The related check that keeps seeded content from admitting it is seeded reads the sense of a word rather than the token now: a water sample, a sample room and a sample unit are the trade meaning and are allowed, while sample data and the rest of that family are still refused, and where a standard has its own word for a thing the seed uses the standard's word.

A row of smaller repairs across the screens. A deadline resolves the party it names instead of printing Unassigned, since three writers put three kinds of value in that column and only one of them was ever looked up, and the punch list seeder puts the main contractor on every item, so a whole screen read as unowned work. A programme that crosses a new year prints the year, exactly when the dates on screen do not all fall inside one, so two rows reading 20 Jan can no longer be twelve months apart with nothing to tell them apart. A meeting shows its status as a word rather than as lowercase English in all languages, and a draft can be scheduled. A photo can be edited into the category it was uploaded with, after the module stated its photo categories in three places and the edit path was the one that had not heard of the category the gallery already offered with its own badge and a translated label. Change order reasons are the ones the product actually writes, the vocabulary having been stated in four places that had drifted while two shipped features raised reasons none of them listed. The calendar subscription box hands out the address the server answers rather than an origin and a bare file name that no route has ever served. The command palette and the sidebar stop offering a page whose module is switched off. The wizard that matches model elements stops printing a raw status through an interpolation nobody passed. Two screens that crashed on opening a record, and a third one edit away from joining them, had a hook sitting below an early return. The collapsed explainer folds back under the module name where its own documentation says it goes. A tall insights panel closes from its own bottom edge rather than only from a header that has scrolled away. The on-costs row says what each of its three inputs wants before an estimator starts typing, rather than carrying that only in an accessible label. And the snapshot integrity report flags a column of numbers that arrived as text again, having asked a question that stopped meaning what it meant the day the data library gained a dedicated text type.

The platform reads in 40 languages, up from 29. Estonian, Bengali, Kazakh, Filipino, Urdu, Persian, Hebrew and Greek are new, and Chile, Colombia and Brazil have locales of their own, derived from Spanish and Portuguese and carrying only the words a reader in that country would not use, with everything else resolving through the fallback chain rather than being duplicated for the sake of being present. That derivation was scoped rather than run blind, because a blind pass elsewhere had once turned a cost assembly into a political meeting and put the name of a payment certificate on the bill of quantities filters; here the measurement rules fire only inside the takeoff and bill modules, the two that would have changed grammatical gender were handled rather than ignored, and one term was dropped entirely because in half its strings it names the operation rather than the tool. Portugal flies its own flag now. Adding a language is also no longer a matter of copying English and translating it: English carries about 32000 keys in its own file while a translated locale carries about 36000, because English is supplied at the call site and only reaches the English file when somebody put it there by hand, so a locale built from it silently drops three and a half thousand strings, no gate notices, and the new language simply shows English on those screens forever. No single other locale is a safe template either. The key set for a new language is computed now, and a locale that was built before the target moved can be caught up in one step.

Two translation defects that no check could see are fixed, and both now have a check behind them. Forty two of the 197 case slugs in the Thai file held values copied whole out of the Korean one, 1031 keys in a single contiguous block, and because the published case pages are generated from the application locales the wrong language went straight onto 43 of them. Nine other locales carried the smaller shape of the same thing, one wrong-language word spliced inside an otherwise correct sentence, which is how a homoglyph enters a translation and stays. A value written in an alphabet its own language does not use is a gate now. Estonian had 1298 keys translated from a neighbouring key's English, because the tool that pairs a key with its English source searched a fixed window for the nearest occurrence of the sibling field, and a dense run of same-named sibling fields put that occurrence in the entry next door while a paragraph-length value ran past the window entirely; the tool is fixed and all 1298 are retranslated from the corrected source. The plural forms a language needs are computed from the language rather than assumed from English and are gated, because the translation layer does not fall back inside a language, so a missing form leaves the language altogether and prints the English. The locale count is read out of the registry and compared both ways rather than asserted as a number, so a locale file with no registry entry and a registry entry with no locale file are both caught and adding the next language does not turn a test red for the only line in it that was wrong.

An upgrade started from inside the product stops reporting a failure it has no way to know about. Downloading a release, resolving its dependencies and installing them takes as long as it takes, and over a slow connection that is minutes, but the work ran inside the request that asked for it. The browser gave up at 45 seconds and said the upgrade had failed while it was still running and, in most cases, still going on to succeed. That is the worst of the available answers, because somebody who believes it will start a second upgrade over the top of the first. The wrong sentence was the smaller half of it. The install ran in the event loop of a single worker, so the server answered nothing at all for the whole duration, which meant the one screen that could have said what was happening was also the screen that had stopped responding, and there was no way to tell a stuck upgrade from a slow one. The request starts a job and hands back its identifier now, the work runs off the loop, and the screen asks for the state until there is an answer. One upgrade runs at a time, and asking again while one is in flight returns the job already running rather than starting a second installer against the same packages. The record of a job lives in the memory of the process that ran it, and that is deliberate rather than a shortcut: an upgrade ends by asking for a restart, the restart is what discards the record, and afterwards the installed version answers the question the job was tracking, so there is nothing left worth remembering. An installation running more than one worker cannot share that lock and should turn the route off, which is what a deployment managed by a pipeline wants in any case. An installer that is genuinely stuck is failed after ten minutes rather than left as a spinner, so the wait always resolves into something a person can act on.

The macOS start failure reported against 14.4.0 now has an explanation read off the shipped file, and this release still does not claim it is fixed. Every census of the sidecar archive came back clean, and it was right and reading the wrong file, the raw packer output with two signing passes still between it and a user. Read from the produced application instead, the sidecar carries the hardened runtime with an ad-hoc signature and no entitlements, and that pairing enforces library validation with nothing able to satisfy it, because library validation does not ask whether the process and the file it maps agree about a team, it asks whether the mapped file carries the loader's team or a platform identity, and an ad-hoc file carries neither. So the runtime is not switched on where there is no identity to satisfy it. Two measurements go with it, and they are the part that can be verified from here. The round-trip re-sign prints the identity it leaves behind, because a signature check says a signature is intact and never says whose it is. And the census runs a second time against the sidecar inside the produced application, naming the file that has to have been inspected for the run to count, so the file named in the failure report cannot clear a run by never having been opened; it warns rather than fails while that measurement is new, since it has no healthy baseline yet and a red run there would skip an unrelated job. The census verdict was one-sided as well, catching a member carrying a team identity against a wrapper without one and reporting the reverse as all clear, which is the shape a real signing identity would produce; both directions report now, and a run that could not read enough to decide says which members it could not read. None of this was tested on a Mac from here, so the first proof that the application launches is the next macOS release.

Several gates were measuring something other than what they claim. The guard that pins which test trees a blocking lane runs graded a step naming nineteen files as full coverage of the tree those files live in, because it could not tell a directory argument from a file inside it, so the two trees it records as thinly gated were the two it was reporting as covered, and it was red while sitting in no workflow, which is why nothing said since when. The migration round trip took its coverage from a hand-written list, and a hand-written list covers what somebody remembered to add to it: every migration in this release was absent from it, so the gate had been green all along without executing one of them. The window is derived from the revision graph now, with the old entries kept behind it as a tail so nothing that used to be covered stops being covered, which makes it self maintaining. The comment on the blocking frontend lane carried three numbers and a cause and all four had drifted. And twelve commits in this history open with a stray opening character ahead of the sentence their author actually wrote, because a shell here-string opener written on the same line as the commit command is consumed as the start of the message: it reads correctly while it is being written and wrong in the log forever. The repository already declared a hook that catches it and the hook had never been installed in the working checkout, which it now is.

## [14.6.0] - 2026-08-06

Tabbing across a bill of quantities reaches the quantity cell and stays there. Moving from the unit column to quantity opened the editor and closed it again in the same keystroke, so the cell appeared to blink and then refused to accept typing, and the only way in was the mouse. The unit editor committed on Tab without cancelling the key, which left the same press to be handled a second time by the grid's own Tab handling, and the second move tore down the editor the first had just opened. The columns before it are unaffected because they use stock editors whose Tab handling has always cancelled. Cancelling the key also removes the grid's own move, so each of the three hand-written editors now makes the move itself and follows the modifier: Shift and Tab walks backwards, where before all three walked forwards regardless. The unit editor had no tests at all; it has six now, three of which go red if the cancel is removed.

A register that records who carried out an inspection prints their name rather than an identifier. The column holds a bare thirty-six character string with no foreign key behind it, and three different things write to it: seeded data records an external party, a picker on other screens records a member of the team, and the form on this screen accepts free text because the field asks for a name. Resolving it against any one of those sources leaves the other two blank, which is why it was left unresolved and a page of identifiers reached the screen, the drawer and the spreadsheet export. It resolves against parties first and people second now, and keeps whatever was stored when neither matches, so a typed name still shows as typed and a deleted party still leaves a trace. The lookup runs once per page rather than once per row, and a value that cannot be an identifier never reaches the database, which on PostgreSQL would refuse the comparison and take the whole list with it.

The check that reads what the macOS sidecar carries can no longer clear a file it never opened. It reported a member count and a verdict over the members it could read, and a member it failed to extract fell out of that count in silence, as did one whose signature it could not parse, which was filed as carrying no identity rather than as unknown. Both now fail the check rather than passing quietly, and it accepts the name of a file that has to have been inspected for the run to count, which the release workflow now sets to the framework named in the report we have. This settles nothing about that report; it removes a measurement that read as settling it.

## [14.5.0] - 2026-08-05

Clicking an element in the BIM viewer to see the defects and inspections attached to it works on PostgreSQL. It raised a server error, on every deployment, since the filter was added. The task list accepts a BIM element id and the query behind it asked for JSON array containment, which is the right question, but the column is declared as portable JSON so that SQLite can carry it too, and on that type the containment call compiles to a string comparison rather than to the containment operator. PostgreSQL then refuses the statement outright because the value being compared arrives typed as JSONB, so the request fails rather than returning the wrong rows, which is the better of the two ways for this to go wrong. The same lookup exists a second time for requirements, written later by copying this one, and it carries the cast that makes the containment real along with a comment explaining why the cast is needed. The copy was correct and the original was not, and the comment above the original described the containment it was supposed to be doing rather than what it did. The original carries the cast now, so both spellings of this lookup compile to the containment operator. The test that catches this exists and is not run by any gate, which is being addressed separately.

A contract still in draft can be deleted from the screen it lives on. The rule permitting it has been in the service layer for as long as the feature has existed, refusing anything that has left draft and saying why, and the client function that calls the endpoint was exported and typed. Nothing called it. There was no delete control on any screen, so from outside the product a working endpoint and a deliberate refusal look the same, and it was reported as a refusal. Nothing in the tree could see it either, because an exported function is not an unused one as far as a linter is concerned, the endpoint is routed and covered, and a screen missing a button renders exactly as correctly as a screen that has one. The control sits beside Sign in the contract drawer and appears only while the contract is in draft, behind a confirmation that names what the deletion takes with it rather than asking whether you are sure, in all 29 languages. It is covered by a test that goes red when the draft condition is removed.

The credentials register can be opened from inside the product. The module was installed, routed on the server, permissioned and complete, and no screen led to it, so the only way in was to know the URL, which from outside is indistinguishable from a module that was never installed. It has a route now, a project scoped one beside it, and an entry under People and Assets next to the resources whose qualifications it tracks. It answers what the crew is licensed to do and what the project demands of them, and it reads in all 29 languages rather than in the four the server itself carries.
